unchanged_frozen_unit.section: a b s t r a c t
unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: Lack of access to electricity is one of the major impediments to economic development and the provision of public services in rural/off-grid areas of developing countries. This study examines the drivers and impacts of rural electrification with Solar Photovoltaic (PV) systems in Ethiopia from a cross-sectional study of 605 rural households and direct field examination of 137 solar PVs/lanterns. Multiple linear regression and econometric analyses were used to analyse the data. Findings showed that the use of solar PV systems in rural Ethiopia is growing and its impact appears significant. A solar-electrified rural household could save the consumption of $43.68\mathrm{~L~}$ of kerosene and emission of $107\mathrm{kg}\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ per year compared with a non-electrified one. This reduction in kerosene use and the access to electricity from solar PVs could enable a rural household to save between US\$ 65 and \$75 per year from avoided energy costs and mobile charging expenses. The study finds that Solar PVs could provide rural households with access to electricity for 3 to $5\mathrm{~h~}$ a day, reduce health damage from kerosene lamps; and allow micro-businesses to generate more income. Empirical results from a binomial logit, and multivariate probit analyses revealed that solar PV adoption is strongly influenced by several economic and non-economic factors. However, it was also found that the use and effectiveness of solar PV systems in rural/off-grid Ethiopia is faced with critical challenges from poor quality and counterfeit products in the market, high cost of quality-verified solar products, lack of after-sales maintenance services, and limited access to credit financing sources.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: Most $(91.2\%)$ of the solar users stated that access to convenient, safe, and high-quality lighting was the main reason they purchased the solar technologies. Respondents noted that solar PVs provided them with high-quality lighting on average for 3 to $5\mathrm{~h~}$ a day and enabled them to minimize or avoid the use of kerosene for lighting. Consistent with the findings of Gustavsson and Ellegård (2004) in Zambia, solar-electrified households pointed out that the quality lighting from the solar devices has improved their quality of life considerably. Beyond the access to quality lighting, the effect of solar use in reducing the kerosene consumption and dependence on low-efficiency kerosene wick-lamps was substantial. From the results in Table 4, the average monthly kerosene consumption of a non-electrified (neither grid nor solar) household is $4.46\mathrm{L},$ but this figure drops to $0.47\mathrm{~L~}$ when grid-electrified; and to $0.82\mathrm{~L~}$ when solarelectrified. This means that, grid-electrified and solar-electrified households could reduce kerosene consumption on average by 3.99 L $(89.5\%)$ and $3.64\mathrm{L}\left(81.60\%\right)$ per month respectively compared to non-electrified (neither grid nor solar) households.

original_block_with_source_spans.text: Most $(91.2\%)$ of the solar users stated that access to convenient, safe, and high-quality lighting was the main reason they purchased the solar technologies. Respondents noted that solar PVs provided them with high-quality lighting on average for 3 to $5\mathrm{~h~}$ a day and enabled them to minimize or avoid the use of kerosene for lighting. Consistent with the findings of Gustavsson and Ellegård (2004) in Zambia, solar-electrified households pointed out that the quality lighting from the solar devices has improved their quality of life considerably. Beyond the access to quality lighting, the effect of solar use in reducing the kerosene consumption and dependence on low-efficiency kerosene wick-lamps was substantial. From the results in Table 4, the average monthly kerosene consumption of a non-electrified (neither grid nor solar) household is $4.46\mathrm{L},$ but this figure drops to $0.47\mathrm{~L~}$ when grid-electrified; and to $0.82\mathrm{~L~}$ when solarelectrified. This means that, grid-electrified and solar-electrified households could reduce kerosene consumption on average by 3.99 L $(89.5\%)$ and $3.64\mathrm{L}\left(81.60\%\right)$ per month respectively compared to non-electrified (neither grid nor solar) households.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: Interestingly household income does not seem to influence kerosene consumption of the households significantly. This may suggest that even richer households who could afford grid electricity connection or solar PV, consume kerosene in quantities not significantly different from poorer ones. However, this could be in part due to unreliable supply and limited access to grid electricity, limited power generation capacity of solar PVs and/or lack of access to solar PVs especially in remote and off-grid areas with undeveloped road networks and PV markets. On the other hand, households living both in Boloso-sore and Aleta-wondo district appear to consume significantly higher quantities of kerosene $\beta52=0.726$ and $\beta53=0.312$ respectively) compared to households in Mirab-abaya (reference category). This supports our earlier findings in Tables 2 and 3 that substantial differences exist among sample households in the four districts with respect to gridconnection, solar adoption, income, and other unobserved differences. In summary, though the estimates of the regression analysis above may not account for all unobserved differences among households within each district, it confirms that solar PV can lead to substantial reduction in kerosene consumption of user households compared to nonelectrified ones.

This supports our earlier findings in Tables 2 and 3 that substantial differences exist among sample households in the four districts with respect to gridconnection, solar adoption, income, and other unobserved differences.

In summary, though the estimates of the regression analysis above may not account for all unobserved differences among households within each district, it confirms that solar PV can lead to substantial reduction in kerosene consumption of user households compared to nonelectrified ones.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: Under a simplified assumption that one million of the 1.1 million solar lighting devices disseminated in Ethiopia up until 2016 are functional or have been replaced by new solar PV products, the results in Table 4 suggest that Ethiopia could avoid the import of 43.68 million L of kerosene and save up to ETB 1.3 billion (US\$ 48 million) per year. This equates to a reduction in Ethiopia's annual import of kerosene oil (295 million L) and spending (US\$ 177 million) by about $15\%$ . For the largely poor country, this financial savings amounts to considerable assistance to the national and household economy and provision of critical public services. Given the high cost of conventional grid expansion in Ethiopia's rugged terrain, the results suggest that promoting solar electrification in rural and off-grid areas even with government subsidies is a viable option. In agreement with our findings, a study be Grimm et al. (2016) in rural Rwanda suggested that, compared to the high-cost grid infrastructure investments, solar PVs are the preferable solutions for mass electrification in off-grid/rural areas of Africa.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: Conversely, factors such as distance to market, access to gridelectricity, price of solar PV and kerosene consumption are negatively and strongly correlated with household's solar PV ownership. unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: More interestingly however, the estimated coefficients in Tables 11 and 12 illustrate that the solar adoption decision of rural households is significantly and negatively influenced by access to grid-electricity, cost of solar PVs, kerosene consumption, distance to market, household size, biogas ownership, and location (Aleta-wondo, and Boloso-sore). As was also discussed by Giri and Goswami (2017) in Nepal, access to grid electricity makes the adoption of solar PVs significantly unlikely. The reason is that households that are already connected to the grid are paying electricity bills and therefore are less likely to purchase solar PVs which would require additional spending. Beyond the cost factor, Karakaya and Sriwannawita (2015) noted that grid-connected households may perceive solar PV as having low level of use with limited durability, and hence not worthy of high investment.

As such, the negative and statistically significant coefficient estimate for the Price of solar PV in both models shows that with increase in cost of solar PV the probability of solar PV adoption decreases significantly. One possible explanation for the negative association between kerosene consumption and solar PV adoption could be that larger quantity kerosene use is related to low-income households and those residing in relatively remote areas with little access to market centres and therefore are less likely to adopt solar PV systems. As was also shown by the correlation test results in Table 10, the strong barrier from high cost of solar PVs (low-income) and limited access to credit financing is more apparent in Boloso-sore district where adoption of solar PV technology is negatively and significantly associated with the district, compared to Mirab-abaya district.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: Comparing the factors influencing solar PV adoption decision with that of grid-electricity and kerosene lamps in the MVP model provides a valuable insight. The higher the level of education of the household, the more likely is the household to adopt grid-electricity. While this accords to previous studies that showed positive and significant relationship between clean lighting energy use and education level of the household-head (e.g. Lay et al., 2013; Rahut et al., 2017), education level of the household does not seem to influence solar adoption significantly in this study, though positive. This could be due to the strong influence of other drivers such as income and accessibility (market) of solar PVs than the education level of the household per se. The probability of adoption of both solar PV and grid-electricity decreases with increase in the distance to market (town). The reason is that in the context of rural Ethiopia, access to grid electricity is higher in areas closer to town than in remote villages. Moreover, the cost of solar installation (transportation cost in particular) is much higher for households distant to town (market) than those closer.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: The aim of this study was to assess and empirically analyse the impacts of stand-alone solar PV systems on rural household energy access, socio-economic development, and the environment in rural southern Ethiopia. The findings showed that the uptake of solar PV/PicoPV systems in rural southern Ethiopia is growing fairly quickly. The most important benefit of solar lighting was the access to clean and quality lighting, and basic electricity; and the resultant reduction in household kerosene consumption for lighting. The study finds that the kerosene consumption of a solar-electrified rural household may decrease on average by $3.64\mathrm{~L~}(81.6\%)$ per month compared to non-electrified ones (neither grid nor solar electrified). The access to solar PV lighting and basic electricity from solar home systems and lanterns could also enable a solar-electrified household to save $\mathrm{US}\$65–$ per year from reduced energy costs and avoided mobile charging fees. Considering the high capital cost of grid expansion to rural/off-grid areas in Ethiopia, the findings present strong evidence to promote the large-scale adoption and utilization of solar PVs systems through introducing additional enabling policy measures such as subsidies and soft loans.

original_block_with_source_spans.text: The aim of this study was to assess and empirically analyse the impacts of stand-alone solar PV systems on rural household energy access, socio-economic development, and the environment in rural southern Ethiopia. The findings showed that the uptake of solar PV/PicoPV systems in rural southern Ethiopia is growing fairly quickly. The most important benefit of solar lighting was the access to clean and quality lighting, and basic electricity; and the resultant reduction in household kerosene consumption for lighting. The study finds that the kerosene consumption of a solar-electrified rural household may decrease on average by $3.64\mathrm{~L~}(81.6\%)$ per month compared to non-electrified ones (neither grid nor solar electrified). The access to solar PV lighting and basic electricity from solar home systems and lanterns could also enable a solar-electrified household to save $\mathrm{US}\$65–$ per year from reduced energy costs and avoided mobile charging fees. Considering the high capital cost of grid expansion to rural/off-grid areas in Ethiopia, the findings present strong evidence to promote the large-scale adoption and utilization of solar PVs systems through introducing additional enabling policy measures such as subsidies and soft loans.

source_spans.text: The aim of this study was to assess and empirically analyse the impacts of stand-alone solar PV systems on rural household energy access, socio-economic development, and the environment in rural southern Ethiopia.
The findings showed that the uptake of solar PV/PicoPV systems in rural southern Ethiopia is growing fairly quickly.
The most important benefit of solar lighting was the access to clean and quality lighting, and basic electricity; and the resultant reduction in household kerosene consumption for lighting.

The study finds that the kerosene consumption of a solar-electrified rural household may decrease on average by $3.64\mathrm{~L~}(81.6\%)$ per month compared to non-electrified ones (neither grid nor solar electrified).

The access to solar PV lighting and basic electricity from solar home systems and lanterns could also enable a solar-electrified household to save $\mathrm{US}\$65–$ per year from reduced energy costs and avoided mobile charging fees.

Considering the high capital cost of grid expansion to rural/off-grid areas in Ethiopia, the findings present strong evidence to promote the large-scale adoption and utilization of solar PVs systems through introducing additional enabling policy measures such as subsidies and soft loans.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: Beyond quality lighting and reduced energy costs, the findings also showed that a solar-electrified household could save the emissions of on average $2.72\mathrm{kg}$ of Black Carbon and $107\mathrm{kg}$ of ${\mathrm{CO}}_{2}$ per year compared to a non-electrified household. This suggests that solar PVs are not only viable solutions for rural electrification but may also play an important role in reducing GHGs emissions and the associated indoor pollution and health damages of traditional kerosene wick lamps. The results also revealed that SHSs could create new income-generating opportunities and increase incomes of existing small-businesses. Yet, it was also found that the success and effectiveness of solar PV systems in rural Ethiopia faces major challenges from poor-quality (counterfeit) products in the market, high cost of quality-verified products, lack of aftersales maintenance service, and limited access to quality-verified solar products and credit financing services.

unchanged_frozen_unit.section: a b s t r a c t
unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: Lack of access to electricity is one of the major impediments to economic development and the provision of public services in rural/off-grid areas of developing countries. This study examines the drivers and impacts of rural electrification with Solar Photovoltaic (PV) systems in Ethiopia from a cross-sectional study of 605 rural households and direct field examination of 137 solar PVs/lanterns. Multiple linear regression and econometric analyses were used to analyse the data. Findings showed that the use of solar PV systems in rural Ethiopia is growing and its impact appears significant. A solar-electrified rural household could save the consumption of $43.68\mathrm{~L~}$ of kerosene and emission of $107\mathrm{kg}\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ per year compared with a non-electrified one. This reduction in kerosene use and the access to electricity from solar PVs could enable a rural household to save between US\$ 65 and \$75 per year from avoided energy costs and mobile charging expenses. The study finds that Solar PVs could provide rural households with access to electricity for 3 to $5\mathrm{~h~}$ a day, reduce health damage from kerosene lamps; and allow micro-businesses to generate more income. Empirical results from a binomial logit, and multivariate probit analyses revealed that solar PV adoption is strongly influenced by several economic and non-economic factors. However, it was also found that the use and effectiveness of solar PV systems in rural/off-grid Ethiopia is faced with critical challenges from poor quality and counterfeit products in the market, high cost of quality-verified solar products, lack of after-sales maintenance services, and limited access to credit financing sources.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: Descriptive statistics and cross-tabulations were used to determine solar PV adoption rates and summarize explanatory variables. Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) was used to determine the significance of variations in mean kerosene consumptions between grid-electrified, solarelectrified, and non-electrified (neither grid nor solar) households. The average kerosene consumptions of non-electrified households were compared with the consumption of grid, and solar-electrified ones to estimate the kerosene consumption and energy expenditure savings of households from solar PVs and lanterns. Kerosene to Black Carbon (BC) and ${\mathrm{CO}}_{2}$ emission conversion factors of $62.33~\mathrm{g/L}$ (Lam et al., 2012a) and $2.45~\mathrm{kg/L}$ (Chaurey & Kandpal, 2010) respectively were applied to estimate annual BC and ${\mathrm{CO}}_{2}$ emission reductions of solar users. In addition, a score ranking method is used to assess the benefits of solar electrification as perceived by rural households. To that effect, the most important benefits of solar products were first established from key informant interviews and secondary sources.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: Most $(91.2\%)$ of the solar users stated that access to convenient, safe, and high-quality lighting was the main reason they purchased the solar technologies. Respondents noted that solar PVs provided them with high-quality lighting on average for 3 to $5\mathrm{~h~}$ a day and enabled them to minimize or avoid the use of kerosene for lighting. Consistent with the findings of Gustavsson and Ellegård (2004) in Zambia, solar-electrified households pointed out that the quality lighting from the solar devices has improved their quality of life considerably. Beyond the access to quality lighting, the effect of solar use in reducing the kerosene consumption and dependence on low-efficiency kerosene wick-lamps was substantial. From the results in Table 4, the average monthly kerosene consumption of a non-electrified (neither grid nor solar) household is $4.46\mathrm{L},$ but this figure drops to $0.47\mathrm{~L~}$ when grid-electrified; and to $0.82\mathrm{~L~}$ when solarelectrified. This means that, grid-electrified and solar-electrified households could reduce kerosene consumption on average by 3.99 L $(89.5\%)$ and $3.64\mathrm{L}\left(81.60\%\right)$ per month respectively compared to non-electrified (neither grid nor solar) households.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: Interestingly household income does not seem to influence kerosene consumption of the households significantly. This may suggest that even richer households who could afford grid electricity connection or solar PV, consume kerosene in quantities not significantly different from poorer ones. However, this could be in part due to unreliable supply and limited access to grid electricity, limited power generation capacity of solar PVs and/or lack of access to solar PVs especially in remote and off-grid areas with undeveloped road networks and PV markets. On the other hand, households living both in Boloso-sore and Aleta-wondo district appear to consume significantly higher quantities of kerosene $\beta52=0.726$ and $\beta53=0.312$ respectively) compared to households in Mirab-abaya (reference category). This supports our earlier findings in Tables 2 and 3 that substantial differences exist among sample households in the four districts with respect to gridconnection, solar adoption, income, and other unobserved differences. In summary, though the estimates of the regression analysis above may not account for all unobserved differences among households within each district, it confirms that solar PV can lead to substantial reduction in kerosene consumption of user households compared to nonelectrified ones.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: Under a simplified assumption that one million of the 1.1 million solar lighting devices disseminated in Ethiopia up until 2016 are functional or have been replaced by new solar PV products, the results in Table 4 suggest that Ethiopia could avoid the import of 43.68 million L of kerosene and save up to ETB 1.3 billion (US\$ 48 million) per year. This equates to a reduction in Ethiopia's annual import of kerosene oil (295 million L) and spending (US\$ 177 million) by about $15\%$ . For the largely poor country, this financial savings amounts to considerable assistance to the national and household economy and provision of critical public services. Given the high cost of conventional grid expansion in Ethiopia's rugged terrain, the results suggest that promoting solar electrification in rural and off-grid areas even with government subsidies is a viable option. In agreement with our findings, a study be Grimm et al. (2016) in rural Rwanda suggested that, compared to the high-cost grid infrastructure investments, solar PVs are the preferable solutions for mass electrification in off-grid/rural areas of Africa.

original_block_with_source_spans.text: Under a simplified assumption that one million of the 1.1 million solar lighting devices disseminated in Ethiopia up until 2016 are functional or have been replaced by new solar PV products, the results in Table 4 suggest that Ethiopia could avoid the import of 43.68 million L of kerosene and save up to ETB 1.3 billion (US\$ 48 million) per year. This equates to a reduction in Ethiopia's annual import of kerosene oil (295 million L) and spending (US\$ 177 million) by about $15\%$ . For the largely poor country, this financial savings amounts to considerable assistance to the national and household economy and provision of critical public services. (2016) in rural Rwanda suggested that, compared to the high-cost grid infrastructure investments, solar PVs are the preferable solutions for mass electrification in off-grid/rural areas of Africa.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: According to the mean score rankings calculated, access to quality lighting is the primary benefit households obtain from solar products with a weighted mean score value of 4.08. The second most important benefit of solar PVs is the access to electricity for charging mobile phones and powering radios. Based on the data collected from solar users, it was estimated that the use of solar PVs has avoided the mobile charging expenses of a single household on average by ETB 40–60 per month (ETB 480–720 per year). Reductions in kerosene consumption and the resultant lighting fuel expenditure savings is ranked third, which reinforces our earlier finding that a solar-user household saves on average ETB 106 per month (ETB 1278 per year) from avoided energy costs compared with a non-electrified household. These figures indicate that a SHS/PicoPV user household in rural southern Ethiopia could save a total of between ETB 1758 and 1998 (US\$ 65–\$75) per year from reduced energy costs and avoided mobile charging expenses.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: Subsequently, factors driving, and hindering household's adoption decision of solar PV systems were examined by applying two econometric analysis models, binomial logit and multivariate probit (MVP). For the multivariate analysis, three dichotomous dependent variables - grid-electricity, solar PV, and traditional kerosene wick lamp (non-electrified) - were included in the model. The multivariate probit model was preferred over other models such as multivariate logistic regression for the reason that it enables us to predict the influence of each predictor variable on the probability of adoption of grid-electricity, solar PV, and kerosene (non-electrified) jointly while allowing the three binary adoption decisions to be potentially correlated or interdependent. Tables 11 and 12 present results of the binomial logit and MVP models respectively.

Akin to the findings in the binomial logit model, the results of the MVP model confirmed that solar adoption decision of households is positively and significantly influenced by income, access to credit facility, number of children enrolled in school and the location (Cheha) of the household. Moreover, the MVP outputs indicate that solar adoption is positively influenced by land holding size, a proxy variable for income. These results suggest that households with higher income levels are more likely to invest in solar PVs than their poorer counterparts. In line with our results, previous studies (Guta, 2018; Lay et al., 2013; Komatsu et al., 2011) in Ethiopia, Kenya, and Bangladesh respectively reported that increase in household income is positively and significantly associated with increase in the likelihood of solar adoption.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: More interestingly however, the estimated coefficients in Tables 11 and 12 illustrate that the solar adoption decision of rural households is significantly and negatively influenced by access to grid-electricity, cost of solar PVs, kerosene consumption, distance to market, household size, biogas ownership, and location (Aleta-wondo, and Boloso-sore). As was also discussed by Giri and Goswami (2017) in Nepal, access to grid electricity makes the adoption of solar PVs significantly unlikely. The reason is that households that are already connected to the grid are paying electricity bills and therefore are less likely to purchase solar PVs which would require additional spending. Beyond the cost factor, Karakaya and Sriwannawita (2015) noted that grid-connected households may perceive solar PV as having low level of use with limited durability, and hence not worthy of high investment.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: Despite the sharp decline in the global price of solar PV modules in recent years, the high upfront cost of solar PV systems remains as one of the major barriers for solar technology adoption in many developing countries (Karakaya & Sriwannawita, 2015). As such, the negative and statistically significant coefficient estimate for the Price of solar PV in both models shows that with increase in cost of solar PV the probability of solar PV adoption decreases significantly. One possible explanation for the negative association between kerosene consumption and solar PV adoption could be that larger quantity kerosene use is related to low-income households and those residing in relatively remote areas with little access to market centres and therefore are less likely to adopt solar PV systems. As was also shown by the correlation test results in Table 10, the strong barrier from high cost of solar PVs (low-income) and limited access to credit financing is more apparent in Boloso-sore district where adoption of solar PV technology is negatively and significantly associated with the district, compared to Mirab-abaya district.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: Comparing the factors influencing solar PV adoption decision with that of grid-electricity and kerosene lamps in the MVP model provides a valuable insight. The higher the level of education of the household, the more likely is the household to adopt grid-electricity. While this accords to previous studies that showed positive and significant relationship between clean lighting energy use and education level of the household-head (e.g. Lay et al., 2013; Rahut et al., 2017), education level of the household does not seem to influence solar adoption significantly in this study, though positive. This could be due to the strong influence of other drivers such as income and accessibility (market) of solar PVs than the education level of the household per se. The probability of adoption of both solar PV and grid-electricity decreases with increase in the distance to market (town). The reason is that in the context of rural Ethiopia, access to grid electricity is higher in areas closer to town than in remote villages. Moreover, the cost of solar installation (transportation cost in particular) is much higher for households distant to town (market) than those closer.

original_block_with_source_spans.text: Comparing the factors influencing solar PV adoption decision with that of grid-electricity and kerosene lamps in the MVP model provides a valuable insight. The higher the level of education of the household, the more likely is the household to adopt grid-electricity. While this accords to previous studies that showed positive and significant relationship between clean lighting energy use and education level of the household-head (e.g. Lay et al., 2013; Rahut et al., 2017), education level of the household does not seem to influence solar adoption significantly in this study, though positive. This could be due to the strong influence of other drivers such as income and accessibility (market) of solar PVs than the education level of the household per se. The probability of adoption of both solar PV and grid-electricity decreases with increase in the distance to market (town). The reason is that in the context of rural Ethiopia, access to grid electricity is higher in areas closer to town than in remote villages. Moreover, the cost of solar installation (transportation cost in particular) is much higher for households distant to town (market) than those closer.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: The aim of this study was to assess and empirically analyse the impacts of stand-alone solar PV systems on rural household energy access, socio-economic development, and the environment in rural southern Ethiopia. The findings showed that the uptake of solar PV/PicoPV systems in rural southern Ethiopia is growing fairly quickly. The most important benefit of solar lighting was the access to clean and quality lighting, and basic electricity; and the resultant reduction in household kerosene consumption for lighting. The study finds that the kerosene consumption of a solar-electrified rural household may decrease on average by $3.64\mathrm{~L~}(81.6\%)$ per month compared to non-electrified ones (neither grid nor solar electrified). The access to solar PV lighting and basic electricity from solar home systems and lanterns could also enable a solar-electrified household to save $\mathrm{US}\$65–$ per year from reduced energy costs and avoided mobile charging fees. Considering the high capital cost of grid expansion to rural/off-grid areas in Ethiopia, the findings present strong evidence to promote the large-scale adoption and utilization of solar PVs systems through introducing additional enabling policy measures such as subsidies and soft loans.

unchanged_frozen_unit.raw_text: Beyond quality lighting and reduced energy costs, the findings also showed that a solar-electrified household could save the emissions of on average $2.72\mathrm{kg}$ of Black Carbon and $107\mathrm{kg}$ of ${\mathrm{CO}}_{2}$ per year compared to a non-electrified household. This suggests that solar PVs are not only viable solutions for rural electrification but may also play an important role in reducing GHGs emissions and the associated indoor pollution and health damages of traditional kerosene wick lamps. The results also revealed that SHSs could create new income-generating opportunities and increase incomes of existing small-businesses. Yet, it was also found that the success and effectiveness of solar PV systems in rural Ethiopia faces major challenges from poor-quality (counterfeit) products in the market, high cost of quality-verified products, lack of aftersales maintenance service, and limited access to quality-verified solar products and credit financing services.
